text:
This replacement slide makes the literature review more concrete and citation anchored.
Lee and See (2004) frame trust in automation as appropriate reliance, which is a useful starting point because the question is not whether people simply trust AI, but whether they rely on it appropriately.
The advice-taking literature shows that people often discount external advice and overweight their own judgment. That matters because Paper 2 studies self judgment versus AI judgment as competing decision sources.
Algorithm aversion and appreciation provide the immediate empirical background. Dietvorst, Simmons, and Massey (2015) show that people can reject algorithms after seeing them err, while Logg, Minson, and Moore (2019) show that algorithmic advice can also be appreciated in some contexts. So the point is not a fixed dislike of algorithms.
EWA then provides the learning language: choices in repeated settings can reflect attraction updating from prior feedback. This is why Paper 2 shifts the unit of analysis from one-shot adoption to a repeated reliance path.
Full APA references used: Lee, J. D., & See, K. A. (2004). Trust in automation: Designing for appropriate reliance. Human Factors, 46(1), 50-80. Dietvorst, B. J., Simmons, J. P., & Massey, C. (2015). Algorithm aversion: People erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(1), 114-126. Logg, J. M., Minson, J. A., & Moore, D. A. (2019). Algorithm appreciation: People prefer algorithmic to human judgment. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 151, 90-103. Yaniv, I., & Kleinberger, E. (2000). Advice taking in decision making: Egocentric discounting and reputation formation. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 83(2), 260-281. Bonaccio, S., & Dalal, R. S. (2006). Advice taking and decision-making: An integrative literature review, and implications for the organizational sciences. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 101(2), 127-151. Camerer, C., & Ho, T.-H. (1999). Experience-weighted attraction learning in normal form games. Econometrica, 67(4), 827-874.
